Hi, I’m Ane Liv Berthelsen [she/her], a marine biologist working in the fields of molecular and behavioral ecology. Here you’ll find my current research, publications and illustrations.

I hold a PhD in molecular and computational biology from the Evolutionary Population Genetics group, the Hoffman lab, at Bielefeld University, Germany. My research explored density from the concept of how individuals perceive it to its effects on fitness traits, transcriptomic profiles, predation risk and a broad range of phenotypic traits of Antarctic fur seals (Arctocephalus gazella). Thus, I employed a broad range of computational frameworks from bioinformatic pipelines to Bayesian hierarchical modelling.
I am currently wrapping up projects from my PhD investigating the drivers behind phenotypic trait variation in Antarctic fur seals and exploring a pausible link between plasticity and fitness.
I am open for opportunities in Copenhagen from January 2027.

title: Recognizing and marshalling the pre-publication error correction potential of open data for more reproducible science

title: Recognizing and marshalling the pre-publication error correction potential of open data for more reproducible science
text:
Behind the scenes
This project arose from a journal club at Bielefeld University discussing the paper by I. Berberi & D.G. Roche https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-022-01879-9. The original paper aimed to evaluate whether journals’ mandatory open data policies increase the potential for error correction. Berberi & Roche concluded that there was “no evidence that mandatory open data policies increase error correction.
To this, R.C. Chen and I raised the point that by counting error corrections and retractions after publication, the original paper overlooked what may be the most important aspect of open data policies: their potential to facilitate error correction before publication.

title: Recognizing and marshalling the pre-publication error correction potential of open data for more reproducible science
text:
Key takeaways
Pre-submission error correction: Researchers are likely to review their data and code more thoroughly when they know that these materials will be made available for others to inspect.
Post-submission error correction: Making data and code available during peer review can increase the opportunity to detect and correct errors before publication.
Overall, this Matters Arising comment emphasizes the potential for open data and code policies to facilitate error correction throughout the publication process, especially pre-publication, thereby improving the reliability of the scientific literature.







NoteCitation & Reference



If you reference or build upon this work, please cite the original paper:
Chen, R.S., Berthelsen, A.L., Lamartinière, E.B. et al. Recognizing and marshalling the pre-publication error correction potential of open data for more reproducible science. Nat Ecol Evol 7, 1597–1599 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-023-02152-3

title: Fine-scale spatiotemporal predator–prey interactions in an Antarctic fur seal colony

title: Fine-scale spatiotemporal predator–prey interactions in an Antarctic fur seal colony
text:
Behind the scenes
The Antarctic fur seal has been extensively studied over the past four decades on Bird Island, South Georgia. However, little reseach has focused on the predator-prey interactions within the colony.Traditional methods can only capture snapshots, making it nearly impossible observe rare encounters.
To overcome this, we set up time-lapse cameras capturing minute-by-minute images across an entire breeding season. To analyze this dataset, we trained a hierarchical YOLO-based neural network capable of identifying adult male fur seals, adult females, pups, and three key avian predator–scavengers: giant petrels, brown skuas, and snowy sheathbills. This resulted in millions of data points mapping fine-scale spatial interactions across time.

title: Fine-scale spatiotemporal predator–prey interactions in an Antarctic fur seal colony
text:
What we tested
First, we tested whether our automatically generated observations matched the known phneology of the species of interest. Second, we investigated spatial associations among Antarctic fur seals, and between them and their associated predator-scavengers.
Avian predator-scavengers are naturally drawn to seal colonies by the abundance of food resources during breeding season. We used the physical proximity between fur seal pups and avian predators as a proxy for predation risk. Historically, the adult male Antarctic fur seal has been the main cause of pup mortality, thus we expected that the pups would try to physically avoid both adult males and their predators. Since that adult females should be invested in the survival of their offspring, we expected that pups could reduce their predation risk (increase distance to nearest predator) by staying close to adult females.

title: Fine-scale spatiotemporal predator–prey interactions in an Antarctic fur seal colony
text:
Key takeaways
Automated accuracy: Detections closely matched established phenology, proving that remote time-lapse setups can reliably monitor remote wildlife colonies.
Spatial avoidance: Pups actively clustered near other pups and adult females while maintaining distance from avian predators and territorial males.
The “Shield” effect: Proximity to adult fur seals of both sexes significantly reduced a pup’s risk of predator proximity. Meanwhile, being close to other pups did not lower predation risk.
Overall, this project emphasizes how remote observation can unlock insights into wildlife behaviour without disturbing sensitive natural habitats.







NoteCitation & Reference



If you reference or build upon this work, please cite the original paper:
Ane Liv Berthelsen, Johannes Bartl, Alexander Winterl, Cameron Fox-Clarke, Jaume Forcada, Rebecca Nagel, Ben Fabry, Joseph Ivan Hoffman; Fine-scale spatiotemporal predator–prey interactions in an Antarctic fur seal colony. R. Soc. Open Sci. 1 May 2026; 13 (5): 250931. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.250931
